name: Mandelic acid deodorant (Lume)

lead: Mandelic acid deodorants aim to keep underarms smelling fresh without aluminium, using an acid formula instead of fragrance or antiperspirant salts. Lume is the best-known brand and sells it as a whole-body deodorant.

Body odor comes from skin bacteria breaking down apocrine sweat, which acid-based deodorants are described as interfering with by keeping the skin surface acidic. Mandelic acid has a long record in chemical peels, but no published study has tested it as a deodorant. They do not reduce sweating.

paras: Applied to clean, dry skin like any deodorant, on underarms or other odor-prone areas, as a daily product.
Acids can irritate skin, and underarm skin is sensitive. Deodorants are regulated as cosmetics in the US, and no product-specific safety trials were located.

angle.text: Mandelic acid deodorants, best known through Lume, use an acid-based formula instead of aluminium to keep odor bacteria down. Mandelic acid has a long record in chemical peels; no deodorant trials exist.

lead: Mandelic acid deodorant refers to underarm and body deodorants built around mandelic acid, an aromatic alpha hydroxy acid, rather than around aluminium salts or fragrance. The best-known example is Lume, a brand that markets a "whole body" deodorant and describes the acid-based formula as an odour-control product.[1][2]

Mandelic acid was first isolated in 1831 from bitter almond extract and is widely used in superficial chemical peels and as a pharmaceutical precursor.[3] Body odour arises mainly when skin bacteria break down secretions from apocrine sweat glands, which is the process acid-based deodorants are intended to interfere with.[4][4]

No published clinical trials were found that test mandelic acid deodorants for odour control. The wiki therefore records the product category mainly through its manufacturer's claims and the general chemistry and dermatology of the ingredient.
infobox: Deodorants are regulated as cosmetics; antiperspirants as drugs[1]

paras: Acid-based deodorants aim to keep the skin surface slightly acidic. Wikipedia's deodorant article notes that such products are meant to preserve the skin's mildly acidic "acid mantle", which limits bacterial growth, and that alkaline soaps can disrupt it.[1] Mandelic acid, with a pKa of about 3.4, is a water-soluble crystalline solid.[3]
Unlike antiperspirants, deodorants do not stop sweating. They act on odour, by masking it or by acting on the bacteria that generate it.[1][4]

Lume sells its product under the name "whole body deodorant" and markets it for women, with the manufacturer's site presenting mandelic acid-based odour control for areas beyond the underarm.[2] See the separate entry on Lume whole body deodorant for the brand's wider use and viral popularity.

Mandelic acid is used in superficial chemical peels and is described as suitable across Fitzpatrick skin types.[3] The American Academy of Dermatology has found insufficient evidence to recommend chemical peels, including mandelic acid peels, for acne, and a 2025 JAAD expert review also did not recommend it for acne.[3] These findings concern acne treatment, not underarm odour.

Acids applied to skin can irritate it. Wikipedia lists mandelic acid as moderately toxic if swallowed and as light-sensitive, darkening over time.[3] Dermatology case literature on other underarm mineral products (alum crystals) documents irritant dermatitis, showing that axillary skin can react to topical deodorant ingredients. No product-specific safety studies were located for mandelic acid deodorants.
No studies found. Research on mandelic acid is largely limited to chemical peels and acne, not deodorant use.[3]

lore.intro: Acid deodorants such as Lume are discussed online, particularly on short-video platforms, as an alternative to conventional deodorants. No forum material was available for this entry.

claims.claim: An acid deodorant controls odour by acting on odour-causing bacteria

timeline.event: Ferdinand Ludwig Winckler discovers mandelic acid from bitter almond extract.[3]
Edna Murphey patents Mum, usually cited as the first modern commercial deodorant.[1]
